chapters.title: Chapter 5: Reducing Capital Gains Tax Legally

lessons.title: Basic Exemption Limit, Rebate and Capital Gains: What Salaried Taxpayers Miss

body.text: Your slab, your deductions and the famous ₹12 lakh rebate work on your ordinary income. Capital gains taxed at special rates sit outside all of that, with one valuable exception: your unused basic exemption limit can still soak them up.

children.text: Two people misread this every year. Sushila, a 67-year-old retired teacher in Coimbatore, assumed her small pension meant she owed nothing on a ₹4,00,000 equity gain. Karan, a 33-year-old analyst in Pune with ₹11,00,000 of taxable salary, assumed the rebate that makes income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free would also cover his ₹1,50,000 short-term gain. One of them was almost right, and the other was completely wrong.
Three Levers, Only One Reaches Capital Gains

children.text: The Basic Exemption Limit Can Absorb Gains

markDefs.definition: The slab threshold below which no tax is payable: ₹4 lakh under the new regime for tax year 2026-27. Under the old regime it is ₹2.5 lakh, ₹3 lakh for those aged 60 to 79 and ₹5 lakh for those 80 and above.

body.title: Sushila's Taxable Gain
body.prompt: Sushila's income after standard deduction is ₹2,25,000 against a ₹4,00,000 basic exemption limit, and her long-term equity gain is ₹4,00,000. After both the ₹1.25 lakh exemption and her unused basic exemption, how much of the gain is taxable, in rupees?
body.explanation: ₹4,00,000 − ₹1,25,000 = ₹2,75,000, then less the unused basic exemption of ₹1,75,000 leaves ₹1,00,000. Tax is ₹12,500 before cess, against ₹34,375 if she had ignored the basic exemption adjustment.

body.title: Who Can Use the Unused Limit?
body.question: Which of these can set unused basic exemption against capital gains taxed at special rates?
options: A resident homemaker with ₹1,50,000 of interest income and ₹3,00,000 of equity long-term gains
An NRI in Dubai with no Indian income other than ₹3,00,000 of Indian equity gains
A private limited company with no business income
All of the above, because the limit applies to every taxpayer
body.explanation: Only resident individuals and HUFs can adjust unused basic exemption against special-rate capital gains. Non-residents are specifically excluded, and companies do not have a basic exemption limit at all.

children.text: The Rebate Stops at Ordinary Income

The new regime rebate can make income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free, but two details decide what it does for an investor. The ₹12 lakh threshold is tested on income excluding special-rate capital gains, and the rebate itself can only wipe out tax on ordinary income. It never touches tax on gains under sections 196, 197 and 198.

body.title: Karan's Rebate Reality Check
body.scenario: Karan is in the new regime with ₹11,00,000 of taxable salary after the standard deduction, plus a ₹1,50,000 short-term gain on listed shares. He has read that income up to ₹12 lakh is tax-free and expects to pay nothing.
body.modelAnswer: His slab tax on ₹11,00,000 of salary is ₹50,000. Because the ₹12 lakh threshold is tested without special-rate gains, his ₹11,00,000 salary keeps him eligible, and the rebate of ₹50,000 wipes out that slab tax entirely. But his short-term gain is taxed separately at 20%: ₹1,50,000 × 20% = ₹30,000. Adding 4% cess, he pays ₹31,200. His salary is genuinely tax-free; his trading profit is not.

body.text: Do not confuse the two tests. Special-rate gains are left out when checking whether your income is within ₹12 lakh, which helps you stay eligible. But the rebate then applies only to the tax on your ordinary income. Many salaried investors discover this only when the portal computes a demand after they file.

body.title: What the Rebate Cannot Do
body.textWithBlank: The rebate for incomes up to ₹12 lakh reduces tax on your ordinary income but can never reduce tax on your ___ capital gains.
body.explanation: Gains taxed at the special rates of 20% and 12.5% under sections 196, 197 and 198 stay payable in full, even when your slab tax is reduced to nil by the rebate.

children.text: Section 80C investments, health insurance premiums and home loan interest reduce ordinary income under the old regime. They cannot reduce capital gains taxed at special rates. That changes how the regime choice looks for an investor. Ritu earns ₹9,00,000 of salary, invests ₹1,50,000 in section 80C instruments and has a ₹2,00,000 long-term equity gain.

body.title: Ritu's Total Tax: Old Regime vs New Regime (Including Cess)

children.text: Her capital gains tax is ₹9,750 under either regime, because the ₹1.25 lakh exemption and the 12.5% rate do not depend on the regime. Only the salary side changes: ₹54,600 under the old regime against nil under the new regime after the rebate. Her total falls from ₹64,350 to ₹9,750.

body.label: Regime Choice and Capital Gains
body.context: Capital gains rates, the ₹1.25 lakh exemption and holding periods are identical under both regimes. Only the basic exemption limit differs, which matters when your ordinary income is below it.

children.text: Senior citizens: under the old regime the basic exemption limit is ₹3 lakh from age 60 and ₹5 lakh from age 80, so a retiree with little other income has more room to absorb gains. The new regime has a single ₹4 lakh limit for everyone, with no higher limit by age.

Marginal relief: if your ordinary income slightly exceeds ₹12 lakh under the new regime, marginal relief limits the extra tax so that it does not exceed the extra income. It applies to slab income, not to special-rate gains.
Surcharge: for high incomes, surcharge on capital gains taxed under sections 196, 197 and 198 is capped at 15%, even where other income attracts a higher surcharge rate.
Order of adjustment: where you have both short-term gains taxed at 20% and long-term gains taxed at 12.5%, setting the unused basic exemption against the 20% gains first usually saves more tax.

Capital gains taxed at fixed rates such as 20% and 12.5%, outside the slab system.

80C, 80D and similar deductions cannot reduce special-rate capital gains.
15% maximum surcharge on capital gains under sections 196, 197 and 198.
Capital gains rates and the ₹1.25 lakh exemption are the same under both regimes.

body.title: Check These Before You File
steps: Work out your ordinary income after standard deduction and any deductions you are claiming
If it is below the basic exemption limit and you are a resident, apply the unused part against your gains
Apply the ₹1.25 lakh equity exemption first, then the unused basic exemption
Remember the rebate will not reduce tax on capital gains, so budget for that amount separately
Compare regimes on your salary side alone, since the capital gains tax will be the same either way
For a parent or retired relative with low income, check whether their gains are being taxed unnecessarily

points: Unused basic exemption limit can be set against special-rate capital gains, but only for residents
The ₹1.25 lakh equity exemption is applied first, then any unused basic exemption
The ₹12 lakh rebate threshold is tested excluding special-rate gains, but the rebate never reduces tax on those gains
80C and similar deductions cannot shelter capital gains taxed at special rates
Capital gains tax is the same under both regimes; only the basic exemption limit differs
Surcharge on these gains is capped at 15%, and senior citizens get higher limits only under the old regime
